exam_format: Paper-based; two sections: multiple choice and free response. Administered at school in May. AP Studio Art/Drawing: portfolio submission. AP Research/Seminar: academic paper and oral presentation.
exam_price_notes: $98 per exam; $55 for students with fee reductions; +$40 international surcharge

testing_centers.notes: AP exams are administered at school sites in May. Some international testing available at authorized international centers. Students must be enrolled in the AP course or register independently through their school.

id_requirements: School ID or government-issued photo ID required. Name on registration must match ID exactly.
exam_rules: No electronic devices (including phones and smartwatches) permitted during the exam. Approved calculators allowed for some sections (e.g., AP Calculus, AP Statistics, AP Physics). AP Studio Art and AP Research/Seminar are assessed via portfolio or academic paper rather than a timed written exam. All exams are paper-based (multiple choice + free-response) except AP Computer Science Principles (some digital components).
renewal_options: AP scores never expire; once earned, scores are valid indefinitely.

retake_policy.notes: AP exams are offered once per year in May. Students may retake the exam in a subsequent year; there is no same-year retake. Scores from all attempts are reported to colleges unless the student requests score cancellation.

editorial.meta_description: The AP Music Theory exam, administered by the College Board, tests pitch, scales, chords, harmony, form, and sight-singing across nine content domains.
editorial.overview: AP Music Theory, offered by the College Board, evaluates students' understanding of pitch, scales, chords, harmonic progressions, musical form, and sight-singing. The paper-based exam lasts 180 minutes and includes multiple-choice and free-response sections. Scored on a 1–5 scale, a 3 is the minimum passing score. The fee is $98, with reductions available. Successful candidates may earn credit equivalent to a one- or two-semester introductory college music theory course.
editorial.who_should_take: High-school students who can read and write musical notation, possess basic voice or instrument proficiency, and seek college credit for an introductory music theory course should enroll in AP Music Theory.
editorial.preparation_strategy: Begin by reviewing each of the nine domain outlines in the official course guide. Practice sight-singing daily, complete timed multiple-choice quizzes, and write out harmonic analyses on staff paper. Use AP Classroom resources and free online lessons such as musictheory.net to reinforce scales, chords, and voice-leading. Take full-length practice exams under timed conditions, then review incorrect items to target weak areas before the May test date.

domain_guidance.summary: Domain 1 covers fundamental pitch concepts, including staff notation, clefs, ledger lines, and the construction of major scales and key signatures. It also introduces basic rhythmic values, meter types, tempo markings, and expressive dynamics.

Domain 2 expands on minor scale forms—natural, harmonic, and melodic—while exploring key relationships, interval identification, melodic contour, and register. It also examines texture types such as monophony, homophony, and heterophony, plus syncopation.

Domain 3 introduces diatonic triads and seventh chords, teaching students to identify chord qualities, construct inversions, and apply Roman-numeral analysis. Emphasis is placed on recognizing chord functions within common-practice harmony.

Domain 4 focuses on chord function, cadence types, and four-part (SATB) voice leading in the style of the 18th century. Students learn proper chord spelling, doubling, voicing, and spacing conventions.

Domain 5 examines predominant chords and their role in harmonic progressions. Learners analyze how these chords lead to dominant functions, study specific predominant types, and practice creating cadences that incorporate predominant function.

Domain 6 introduces secondary functions, including secondary dominants and leading-tone chords, and the process of tonicization. Students learn how chords borrow from parallel keys to enrich harmonic progressions.

Domain 7 covers extended and altered harmonies, including ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth chords, as well as altered dominants. Learners practice identifying these chords and part-writing them within four-part textures.

Domain 8 explores musical modes, phrase relationships, and formal structures such as introductions, bridges, verses, choruses, codas, and codettas. Students analyze how these sections create larger forms and convey musical narrative.

Domain 9 emphasizes sight-singing, requiring students to vocalize notated melodies accurately on first reading. Practice includes interval recognition, rhythmic accuracy, pitch maintenance, and interpretive phrasing within an appropriate range.

editorial.exam_day_guidance: Arrive early with a photo ID, several #2 pencils, and an eraser. The paper-based test runs for 180 minutes, beginning with multiple-choice items followed by free-response questions. No calculators or electronic devices are permitted.

faq.question_title: How many questions are on the exam?
faq.answer_text: The AP Music Theory exam consists of a multiple-choice section and a free-response section; the exact number of items varies each year, but together they assess knowledge across all nine domains in the official course guide.

Scores are reported on a 1–5 scale; a score of 3 is the minimum passing level and may qualify students for college credit depending on the institution's policy. A score of 5 indicates the highest level of mastery.

The exam is a three-hour, 180-minute, paper-based assessment administered in May at the student's school under supervised conditions. No calculators, phones, or other electronic devices are permitted in the testing room.

faq.question_title: How much does the exam cost?
faq.answer_text: The exam fee is $98 per student. Students who qualify for fee reductions pay $55, and an additional $40 international surcharge applies where relevant. Schools handle registration and payment through the College Board.

faq.question_title: When is the AP Music Theory exam administered?
faq.answer_text: The AP Music Theory test is scheduled each May during the regular AP testing window; students take it at their school on the date set by the College Board. Specific dates appear on the official AP calendar annually.

faq.question_title: Are there any exam codes I should know?
faq.answer_text: The course is identified as AP Music Theory and is administered by the College Board. There is no separate exam code beyond the standard AP designation used for registration and score reporting.
